strengths: Novel and interesting problem formulation: applying generative world models to simulate OS GUIs, which presents distinct challenges (discrete state transitions, precise cursor localization, long-horizon interactivity) compared to video games.

Well-motivated architectural design: the hierarchical RNN for state tracking paired with a latent diffusion renderer, plus explicit Gaussian cursor position encoding, is a sensible and clearly explained solution to the unique demands of OS simulation.

Multi-stage training pipeline (RNN pretraining, joint training, scheduled sampling, context extension) is thoughtfully designed, with the RNN-pretraining-to-avoid-renderer-ignoring-the-RNN insight being a useful practical contribution.

Substantial engineering effort: search-tree-based agent data collection with Claude, random exploration data to break spurious correlations, 64-way parallel Docker collection (~12TB of data), and detailed hyperparameters in the appendix.
Honest limitations section; code, pretrained model, and an interactive demo are released, supporting reproducibility and follow-up work.

Ablation studies demonstrate the necessity of joint training (blurring without it) and scheduled sampling (error accumulation without it), and cursor-map ablation shows clear quantitative gains (1.6/1.4 pixel error vs. 130/95.8).
weaknesses: No comparison to any external baseline system. Prior work like DIAMOND, GameNGen-style architectures, or even a straightforward transformer-based autoregressive video predictor conditioned on inputs is not evaluated, making it impossible to judge whether the proposed architecture is the right design or merely one that works adequately.

The evaluation set is very small (730 examples, 10 per cluster) and quantitative results are limited: cursor accuracy and a 37.7% state-transition clustering accuracy. The latter metric is custom, weakly defined (matching to 'closest cluster' is not a rigorous notion of correctness), and the authors themselves note off-diagonal predictions may be valid, further undermining the metric's interpretability.

Key functionality fails: fine-grained keyboard/typing interactions (a core part of using an OS, e.g., terminal commands) are not reliably modeled, and resolution is low (512x384). This substantially limits the claim of simulating an 'operating system'; what is demonstrated is closer to desktop navigation simulation.

Significant compute (23,000 GPU-hours) for a proof-of-concept whose demonstrated capabilities (moving a cursor, opening folders/applications) remain modest relative to the resource investment; the paper does not clearly establish what the compute bought beyond the proof of concept.
The real-user finetuning results are deferred entirely to a separate work (Zhang et al., 2025), leaving an advertised contribution unsupported within this paper.

Evaluation is predominantly qualitative (figures of generated sequences); no human study or user-facing evaluation of interactive quality is provided, despite the paper's motivation centered on interactive usability.

Technical novelty of individual components is limited: LSTM state tracking, latent diffusion, scheduled sampling, and DDIM sampling are all established techniques combined together; the Gaussian cursor map is simple though effective.

Some details are vague: the clustering procedure for state-transition evaluation is underspecified, and the RNN parameter count (2.2B) for two 4,096-hidden LSTMs plus attention seems inconsistent or at least unexplained.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely novel and interesting problem: applying interactive world models (previously applied mostly to games) to operating-system GUIs, where discrete state changes, delayed responses, and precise cursor localization pose challenges distinct from game simulation.

The data collection infrastructure is a notable contribution: search-tree-based exploration with a computer-use agent, Bezier-curve-motivated random interactions, and parallelized Docker collection across 64 containers produce a large-scale OS interaction dataset.

The multi-stage training pipeline (RNN pretraining to prevent the renderer from ignoring RNN outputs, joint training, scheduled sampling, context extension, curriculum on challenging transitions) is well motivated, and the ablations qualitatively support the necessity of the joint-training and scheduled-sampling stages.
The Gaussian spatial cursor map is a simple but effective design choice, supported by a large quantitative gap (1.6/1.4 px vs 130/95.8 px error) and a qualitative failure mode analysis (Appendix A).
The paper is candid about limitations (low resolution, unreliable keyboard simulation, 1.8 fps inference, large compute cost), and releases code, model, and a demo.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation is thin. All experiments rest on only 730 evaluation examples, and there are no standard video-quality metrics (FVD/FID/PSNR) or human evaluations to substantiate claims of 'realistic' generation; key claims about visual realism rest on cherry-picked figures.

The central state-transition metric is weak evidence: 37.7% accuracy against an automatically clustered set of 73 categories, with the authors themselves conceding that off-diagonal predictions may be valid. The cluster-matching methodology is ad hoc and unvalidated, making the headline number hard to interpret.

The baseline comparisons are problematic. The 'without cursor map' baseline is an earlier model version trained for fewer steps under different conditions (footnote 5), confounding the comparison; and there is no comparison whatsoever to prior action-conditioned video prediction / world model approaches (e.g., DIAMOND, GameNGen-style architectures) even on the authors' own data, so the architectural choices are not contextualized against alternatives.

The cursor-accuracy evaluation may be circular: the model is explicitly given a Gaussian cursor map during generation, and a regression model reads the rendered cursor back out. The result largely measures whether the renderer faithfully reproduces a signal it was handed, not whether the model understands cursor semantics.

Significance relative to cost is questionable. ~23,000 GPU hours and 4 months of training yield a system at 512x384 resolution, 1.8 fps, that cannot reliably simulate keyboard input — arguably a core part of the motivating vision. The paper is essentially an expensive proof of concept, and the leap to 'generative operating systems' and 'a new computing paradigm' is speculative.

Technical presentation has gaps and inconsistencies: the RNN (2.2B parameters) is stated to dwarf the 263M renderer without justification; the claim that 'predicting clean image' outperforms noise prediction is asserted from limited experiments; some details (URLs, interactive training results) are deferred entirely to other work.
Scope is narrow: a single desktop environment (XFCE) at fixed low resolution with a minimal application set, so generalization claims are unsupported.

strengths: Novel and interesting problem setting: NeuralOS is, to my knowledge, the first attempt to model a full desktop OS GUI as an input-conditioned generative video process, distinct from prior game/world-model simulators (GameNGen, DIAMOND, Genie) that operate on games with simpler, more regular dynamics.

Well-motivated architecture design: the hierarchical two-level LSTM state tracker plus latent diffusion renderer cleanly mirrors the kernel/rendering separation, and the constant per-timestep complexity of the RNN is well-justified for long-horizon interactive simulation.

The multi-stage training pipeline (RNN pretraining via MSE, joint training, scheduled sampling, context extension) addresses real, clearly-diagnosed failure modes (renderer ignoring RNN output, exposure bias, limited context), and the ablations (Figure 6) provide concrete evidence that each stage is necessary.

Thorough data collection effort: search-tree-based agent exploration with Claude computer-use, heuristic-driven random exploration to break spurious correlations, and parallel Docker infrastructure; the discussion of spurious correlations (cursor moving to close button without click) shows good empirical insight.
Strong reproducibility artifacts: code, pretrained model, interactive demo, detailed hyperparameters (Table 1, Appendices D-H), and data collection prompts are all provided.
Honest limitations section acknowledging low resolution, unreliable keyboard modeling, and slow inference speed.
weaknesses: Evaluation is quite limited: only 730 test examples are used, and there is no comparison against any external baseline or alternative architecture (e.g., a transformer-based state tracker, or adapting a game world model like DIAMOND/GameNGen to this data). All comparisons are against ablations of the authors' own system, making it hard to judge whether the chosen architecture is actually the right one for this task.

The state-transition metric is ad hoc: clustering challenging transitions into 73 categories and matching predictions to the nearest cluster yields a 37.7% 'accuracy' whose interpretation is murky; the authors themselves concede off-diagonal predictions may be valid, which undermines the metric's meaning. No standard video prediction metrics (FVD, LPIPS, PSNR/SSIM on non-challenging frames) are reported.

The cursor-position baseline (Figure 5b, ∆x=130) is an 'earlier model version trained for 700K steps under slightly different conditions' (footnote 5), so the central claim about the cursor map's importance rests on a partially confounded comparison; a properly controlled ablation of the same model without the map is needed.

Practical significance is currently modest: 512×384 resolution, 1.8 fps on an H100, unreliable keyboard input, and a minimal, customized application set. The system simulates a heavily simplified OS, so claims about 'simulating operating systems' should be tempered.

Architectural choices are under-analyzed: a 2.2B-parameter RNN paired with a 263M-parameter renderer is surprising and the paper gives little justification or sensitivity analysis for this allocation; nor is the choice of predicting clean images instead of noise (footnote 3) backed by experiments.

Scaling behavior is not studied: with ~17K GPU-hours spent, there is little evidence about how performance scales with data or compute, which matters for assessing whether this approach can ever reach usable fidelity.

Some important details are deferred or missing: finetuning with real-user data is delegated entirely to a different work (Zhang et al., 2025), leaving a claimed contribution unevidenced in this paper.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem framing: first concrete demonstration of simulating a full OS graphical interface (rather than a single game) with a neural generative model, extending the world-model paradigm (GameNGen, DIAMOND) to a domain with delayed, state-dependent, non-Markovian visual transitions.

Technically well-conceived architecture: the two-level LSTM state tracker + diffusion renderer design is well justified by the domain's challenges (long-horizon state like 'is Firefox open', precise cursor rendering), and the Gaussian cursor position map is a simple, effective, and well-ablated solution (1.4-1.6 px error vs ~100+ px without).

Thoughtful multi-stage training pipeline (RNN pretraining to prevent renderer from ignoring the RNN, joint training, scheduled sampling, context extension) with each stage motivated by an identified failure mode and supported by ablations (Figures 4c, 6, Table 4).

Multi-faceted evaluation: cursor localization regression, DBScan-based state-transition matching, application open/close RMSE, human Turing-style evaluation (~chance for cropped clips up to 20s), long-term memory experiment generalizing beyond the 64-frame training context to 256 frames, and a DIAMOND baseline comparison with equalized compute.

Striking Doom result: learning to launch/play/close an application that never existed in the underlying system, via synthetic demonstrations, which is a genuinely interesting proof-of-concept for learned-from-demonstration interfaces.
Strong reproducibility: released code, checkpoints, dataset construction details, full hyperparameters, and a live interactive demo.
weaknesses: Very narrow scope relative to the 'operating system' framing: only 4 applications (Home, Trash, Terminal, Firefox) at 512x384 on a single desktop environment; keyboard input modeling essentially fails (admitted in the paper), so terminal interaction is largely non-functional — the system simulates a desktop launcher more than an OS.

State-transition accuracy of 37.7% is modest, and while the authors argue off-diagonal predictions may be valid due to timing variability, this claim is only qualitatively defended; the evaluation protocol for 'valid but off-diagonal' transitions lacks quantitative rigor.

Methodologically incremental: the core components (latent diffusion, LSTM state tracking, scheduled sampling, curriculum training) are established techniques applied to a new domain; novelty rests primarily on engineering and the domain-specific contributions (cursor map, RNN pretraining), which individually are modest.

Substantial compute cost (~23,000 GPU hours) for a system with limited capability and low resolution; the paper does not convincingly demonstrate that the approach will scale, and inference requires an H100, limiting practical significance.

Some evaluation details are under-specified or potentially confounded: the human evaluation does not state the number of participants or statistical significance; the 'no cursor map' baseline is a different (earlier) model version, weakening the ablation; DIAMOND was trained for only 48 hours vs NeuralOS's multi-month training schedule, even if one comparison is compute-equalized.
The long-term memory claim rests on a single, hand-crafted task (folder presence) with only 500 examples, and the MSE-threshold-based folder detection is a somewhat crude metric.
Additional finetuning with real-user data is deferred to another work (Zhang et al., 2025), leaving a component of the pipeline unevaluated in this paper.

strengths: Ambitious and interesting problem: learning an interactive, action-conditioned simulator of an OS GUI is a novel application setting distinct from game world models, and the paper articulates real challenges (delayed state transitions, precise cursor control, long-horizon memory)
The Doom-from-synthetic-demonstrations experiment is a memorable and genuinely thought-provoking demonstration of learning interfaces from fabricated data

Multi-stage training pipeline (RNN pretraining, joint training, scheduled sampling, context extension) is well-motivated, and the ablations showing blurry RNN-only outputs and error accumulation without scheduled sampling are informative
The authors are transparent about limitations (keyboard fidelity, resolution, inference cost, 23,000 GPU hours) and release code, checkpoints, and a demo
weaknesses: Extremely poor cost-benefit trade-off: ~23,000 GPU hours of training for an environment with only four desktop icons at 512x384 resolution. The system cannot reliably model keyboard inputs or text, which are core to an operating system; the simulated 'OS' is essentially a desktop with four applications

Limited technical novelty: the method is a fairly standard assembly of known components (LSTM state tracker, latent diffusion UNet, Gaussian spatial cursor map, scheduled sampling). The RNN pretraining trick and cursor map are incremental engineering fixes rather than conceptual advances

Weak quantitative results: state-transition accuracy is only 37.7% (vs. 1.4% majority baseline), a number far below what would be usable for any downstream purpose (e.g., training computer-use agents, the paper's motivating application), and the DBSCAN-cluster-based evaluation protocol is ad hoc with unquantified sensitivity

Insufficient baselines: the only comparison is a DIAMOND adaptation trained for 48 hours on a single GPU, i.e., orders of magnitude less compute than the main model (3M+ steps, multi-GPU-months), making the comparison uninformative. No comparisons against stronger recent world models (GameNGen, Genie 3, PAN, transformer variants beyond a memory-usage table)

The human evaluation is small (30 trials per participant per condition) and the headline claim of near-chance distinguishability only holds under cropping; the un-cropped condition shows raters detecting artifacts, and the metric does not measure functional fidelity of interactions

The 'long-term memory beyond training horizon' claim is overstated: folder-presence recall is only 0.52-0.62 for the positive class, barely better than chance for 'Folder Created' cases, and the Doom result primarily shows the model memorizing spliced synthetic sequences rather than genuine compositional generalization
A 2.2B-parameter RNN (10x larger than the renderer) is an unusual and under-analyzed design choice; the paper does not justify why such a large recurrent module is necessary versus alternatives

Significance is unclear: as a 'safe environment for computer-use agents,' a simulator with 37.7% transition accuracy and no keyboard support is not yet useful; as an HCI vision, the contribution amounts to a feasibility demo with limited generalizable methodology

strengths: Novel and compelling problem setting: simulating an OS GUI via action-conditioned frame prediction is a distinct challenge from video-game world models due to delayed responses, spurious correlations, and long-horizon state, and the paper clearly articulates these differences.

Substantial end-to-end system contribution: 122K recorded demonstrations from 64 parallel Docker environments, a 2.2B-parameter hierarchical RNN plus 263M UNet renderer, a four-stage training pipeline (RNN pretraining, joint training, scheduled sampling, context extension), and a real-time (18 fps) interactive demo with public code and checkpoints.

Multi-faceted evaluation: cursor localization (1.4–1.6 px error with the Gaussian cursor map vs. ~100–130 px without), state-transition accuracy (37.7% vs. 1.4% majority), application open/close accuracy (Table 6), a human Turing-style study (near-chance identification for ≤20s clips), and a long-term memory experiment showing folder-state recall at 256 frames beyond the 64-frame training context.

The synthetic Doom demonstration is a genuinely interesting result showing that fabricated demonstrations can be distilled into a usable simulated interface, supporting the broader 'generative interfaces' thesis.

Appendix A provides a reasonable adaptation of DIAMOND as an external baseline under matched compute, and ablations (Figures 4c, 6) support the necessity of the cursor map, joint training, and scheduled sampling.
Good reproducibility: hyperparameter tables, data collection prompts, autoencoder details, and released code/demo/checkpoints; honest limitations and ethics statements.
weaknesses: Narrow scope: only four desktop applications (Home, Trash, Terminal, Firefox), 512×384 resolution, and unreliable keyboard/text modeling; the practical usefulness of the simulator as an agent-training environment remains unproven since text/terminal interactions — central to computer-use agents — are not well supported.

Key evaluation has caveats: the state-transition accuracy of 37.7% relies on DBSCAN-clabeled clusters and the authors themselves note off-diagonal predictions may be valid, making the metric difficult to interpret; the 'no cursor map' baseline is an earlier model version trained under different conditions (700K steps), which weakens the causal claim about the cursor map; the eval set is small (730 examples, 10 per cluster).

Some ablations are missing or incomplete: no controlled comparison for the RNN vs. transformer encoder choice beyond memory footprints (Table 5 measures cost, not quality), and no ablation for Stage 4 context extension or the curriculum training on challenging transitions.

Very high cost (17,000 H200 + 6,000 H100 GPU hours over ~4 months) relative to the demonstrated capability, which constrains reproducibility in practice and raises questions about the efficiency of the design (e.g., why the RNN needs 2.2B parameters).

The 'novel pretraining method' is essentially standard two-stage pretrain-then-finetune with MSE initialization; the framing overstates architectural novelty, and scheduled sampling is adopted from prior work. The main novelty is applying and engineering these components for a new domain.

The 'Additional Finetuning with Real-User Data' section defers all details and results to a different work (Zhang et al., 2025), which is unusual and unverifiable within this paper; claims of improved alignment are therefore unsupported here.

Human evaluation results, while positive for short clips, degrade over longer durations (46.7–50% at 40–60s in the cropped condition is at/below chance), suggesting realism does not hold for longer interactions; the paper does not discuss this trend.
